chief_complaint: expanding bullseye skin rash, fever, and feeling dizzy/fainting post-tick bite
hpi_details: 33M presenting with 12cm annular erythema migrans rash on thigh 2 weeks after camping, fever, arthralgias, and new-onset 2nd degree AV block on ECG.
ideas: He thinks an infected insect or poisonous spider bit him during his camping trip and injected venom into his body.
concerns: He is worried that his fainting spells will cause him to pass out behind the wheel while commuting to work.
expectations: He hopes to receive a prescription for antibiotics or a topical cream to clear up the rash so he can safely return to work tomorrow.

available_results.value: Second-degree atrioventricular block, Mobitz I (Wenckebach), with ventricular rate 46 bpm

clinical_knowledge.topic: Lyme Disease with Carditis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lyme Disease with Carditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes hospital admission with continuous cardiac telemetry and IV antibiotic therapy for Lyme carditis with AV block, transitioning to oral doxycycline once the block resolves, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: expanding bullseye skin rash, fever, and feeling dizzy/fainting post-tick bite
Key HPI features: 33M presenting with 12cm annular erythema migrans rash on thigh 2 weeks after camping, fever, arthralgias, and new-onset 2nd degree AV block on ECG.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.0C, HR 46 (bradycardic, irregular), BP 108/68, RR 16. 12cm annular erythema migrans lesion with central clearing on the thigh; mild cervical lymphadenopathy; mild arthralgias without joint effusion; no meningismus. ECG: new 2nd degree AV block (Mobitz I/Wenckebach pattern). Bloods: two-tier Lyme serology positive (ELISA reactive, confirmatory IgM/IgG Western blot positive); ESR and CRP mildly elevated.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lyme Disease with Carditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cellulitis (non-migrating, tender) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dizziness, fainting, or an irregular heartbeat — suggests Lyme carditis and heart block.
management_principles: Admit for continuous cardiac telemetry monitoring given the AV block, with temporary pacing available if the block is high-grade or the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable

Start IV Ceftriaxone 2g once daily (or IV Penicillin G) for Lyme carditis with AV block; transition to oral Doxycycline 100mg BID once the block resolves or improves, to complete a 14-21 day total course
Avoid permanent pacemaker placement — Lyme-associated AV block is typically reversible with antibiotic therapy and usually resolves within days to weeks
Counsel on tick-bite prevention; note that follow-up serology is not useful for monitoring treatment response, since antibody titers can remain positive for years
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A tick-borne Borrelia burgdorferi infection causing an expanding bullseye rash (erythema migrans), and when it spreads to the heart, can cause conduction block requiring cardiac monitoring.
red_flags: Dizziness, fainting, or an irregular heartbeat — suggests Lyme carditis and heart block

must_ask.say: Have you been camping, hiking, or in wooded areas recently, and did you notice a tick bite?
Does the rash look like an expanding red ring, like a bullseye?
Have you felt dizzy, faint, or noticed your heart beating irregularly?
Any joint pain or flu-like symptoms?
How long ago did the rash appear?

history.answer: I went camping two weeks ago and found a tick bite on my leg, and now this red ring on my thigh keeps spreading, plus I have a fever and feel really dizzy.
It started about a week ago right where the tick bit me on the front of my left thigh, and it has been expanding into a larger ring every day.
It is just that single large ring on my left front thigh; there are no other spots anywhere on my body.
It looks like a red bullseye target with a clearer patch in the center; there are no bumps, blisters, or scabbing.
It does not really itch or hurt at all, though the red ring feels slightly warm when I touch it.
No, it has not faded or moved around; it has been there continuously and slowly getting bigger over the week.
No, I have never had a skin reaction or rash like this in my life.
Yes, I developed a fever of 38 degrees, bad chills, and deep muscle fatigue starting about two days ago.
No sores, blisters, or redness anywhere in my mouth, eyes, or genital area.
No, my skin is not peeling or blistering, and I do not have any dark purple spots or bruises.
My face and throat are not swollen and I am not wheezing, but I have felt extremely dizzy and lightheaded, like I might pass out.
I have not started any new prescription medications, antibiotics, or painkillers lately.
No new laundry detergents, soaps, body washes, cosmetics, or contact with poison ivy.
None of the friends who went camping with me or my family members have any rash or fever.
I went camping in a wooded state park two weeks ago, and when I got home I found a tiny tick attached to my left thigh and pulled it off with tweezers.
No, I have never had eczema, asthma, or seasonal allergies.
Both of my knees and wrists have been stiff and aching for the past couple of days, but my nails look completely normal.
I put a little hydrocortisone cream on the rash two days ago, but it did not make any difference.
I am monogamous with my wife and have had no other sexual partners, and neither of us has ever had genital ulcers or sores.
My heart feels unusually slow and feels like it skips beats, and twice today I almost passed out when I stood up.
The tick bite happened two weeks ago, the rash appeared one week ago, and the fever and dizzy spells began two days ago.
I was camping two weeks ago and noticed a bite on my thigh, so I thought a poisonous spider might have bitten me and spread venom.
I've been feeling so dizzy that I'm terrified I might pass out while driving to work and get into a crash.
I hope you can give me some antibiotics or an ointment to clear this bite up so I can get back to work tomorrow.
I have high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol, but no other chronic health issues.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital before.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure; I do not take any over-the-counter supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I only drink one or two beers socially on weekends.
I work full-time in an office as an accountant and live in a house with my wife.
My father has high blood pressure, but there is no family history of heart block, arrhythmias, or autoimmune diseases.

exam.finding: Temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 46 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute.
Alert 33-year-old male, appears fatigued and flushed, but comfortable at rest without acute respiratory distress.
A 12 cm annular erythema migrans patch with prominent central clearing on the anterior left thigh; no necrosis, desquamation, or purpura.
Mildly enlarged, mobile, non-tender cervical lymph nodes bilaterally; no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Marked bradycardia with an irregular rhythm and dropped beats; normal heart sounds without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal vesicular air entry and no crackles or wheezes.
Mild tenderness on active and passive movement of bilateral wrists and knees, without swelling, erythema, warmth, or joint effusion.
Full active and passive neck flexion without nuchal rigidity; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Oral mucosa and pharynx are moist and pink without ulcers, vesicles, or mucosal enanthem.
Conjunctivae are pink without injection or petechiae, and sclerae are non-icteric.
